arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Medical-Grade vs Convenience Features
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two versions of a home monitoring device concept. Participants view a device description emphasizing medical-grade accuracy (T1) or convenience features (T2). They then indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
arguments.sample: 400 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to see either the accuracy description or the convenience description.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when accuracy is highlighted.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when convenience is highlighted.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for the accuracy version exceeds the convenience version by at least €10, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition built on medical‑grade accuracy. If the difference is less than €10, maintain focus on professional healthcare.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition built on medical‑grade accuracy, leveraging Masimo’s existing reputation and home‑care strategy.
arguments.target_customer: Consumers seeking reliable, safe home monitoring for chronic conditions (e.g., diabetes, COPD) who trust medical‑grade accuracy.
arguments.value_proposition: A line of home‑monitoring devices marketed as medical‑grade, sold directly to consumers at premium prices, with potential for subscription services for ongoing data analysis.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (400 U.S. adults, 10‑week timeline, €15,000 budget) to measure willingness to pay for accuracy versus convenience.
arguments.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for medical‑grade accuracy is uncertain; the test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows willingness to pay for accuracy is significantly lower than for convenience, or if a separate test shows strong demand for subscription services, the recommendation would shift toward a convenience‑focused or service‑focus
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for over‑the‑counter devices without medical‑grade claims, the recommendation would shift toward no expansion.

final.recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition built on medical-grade accuracy, leveraging Masimo’s existing reputation and home-based telemedicine strategy.
final.target_customer: Health-conscious consumers who prioritize medical accuracy for home monitoring, particularly those with chronic conditions or seeking proactive health management.
final.value_proposition: A line of home monitoring devices marketed as medical-grade, offering high accuracy and safety, sold directly to consumers and through retail partners, with potential for premium pricing and recurring revenue through subscription services.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for accuracy versus convenience. If the accuracy emphasis yields at least a 15% higher purchase intent, proceed with a limited consumer launch;
final.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for medical-grade accuracy is uncertain; the test will clarify this. Additionally, the size of the consumer market and competitive landscape remain unknown.
would_change_if: If the test shows a <5% difference in purchase intent between accuracy and convenience, indicating no clear consumer preference, we would reconsider the consumer proposition and focus on professional healthcare.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for convenience features or subscription models, we would shift toward a convenience-driven or service-based consumer offering.

arguments.sample: 400 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to see either the accuracy description or the convenience description.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when accuracy is highlighted.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when convenience is highlighted.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for the accuracy version exceeds the convenience version by at least €10, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition built on medical‑grade accuracy. If the difference is less than €10, maintain focus on professional healthcare.

arguments.recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition built on medical‑grade accuracy, leveraging Masimo’s existing reputation and home‑care strategy.
arguments.target_customer: Consumers seeking reliable, safe home monitoring for chronic conditions (e.g., diabetes, COPD) who trust medical‑grade accuracy.
arguments.value_proposition: A line of home‑monitoring devices marketed as medical‑grade, sold directly to consumers at premium prices, with potential for subscription services for ongoing data analysis.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (400 U.S. adults, 10‑week timeline, €15,000 budget) to measure willingness to pay for accuracy versus convenience.
arguments.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for medical‑grade accuracy is uncertain; the test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows willingness to pay for accuracy is significantly lower than for convenience, or if a separate test shows strong demand for subscription services, the recommendation would shift toward a convenience‑focused or service‑focus

arguments.name: Fashion vs Thermal Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios.
arguments.sample: 300 US adults recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and gender to reflect the target consumer base.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and maximum willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 40% of respondents will express purchase intent for a thermal-regulating PCM garment, and WTP will be at least €50.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% of respondents will express purchase intent for a PCM garment marketed as fashion/status, and WTP will be at least €50.

arguments.decision_rule: If the proportion of respondents who express purchase intent for the thermal scenario exceeds the proportion for the fashion scenario by at least 10 percentage points, adopt T1. If the difference is less than 10 points, adopt T2. If neither meets the threshold, no expansion is recommended.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for thermal comfort in extreme environments, targeting outdoor recreation and aviation. Begin with a limited direct-to-consumer launch of a prototype thermal PCM garment, using the existing B2B brand and technical reputation.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Eco‑Green Messaging
arguments.method: Online choice experiment with between‑subjects design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: (A) Premium‑performance messaging (high‑end NASA‑developed, superior thermal comfort) or (B) Eco‑green messaging (sustainable, reduces energy consumption). They view a product description of the same flexible aerogel blanket and are asked to indicate purchase intent (yes‑no) and maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 400 U.S. homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for income, education, and environmental concern. Randomly assigned 200 to Premium condition, 200 to Eco‑Green condition.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: intent to buy) and maximum price willingness to pay (continuous).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium condition will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Eco‑Green condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Eco‑Green condition will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Premium condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between Premium and Eco‑Green conditions exceeds 5 percentage points and the difference in willingness to pay exceeds €50, we conclude that the premium‑performance message drives higher adoption. If the difference is ≤ 5 points and ≤ €50, we conclude the eco‑green message drives adoption. If neither difference meets the thresholds, we conclude neither message is effective.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for residential insulation that emphasizes premium performance and NASA‑developed quality, using a test offering the aerogel blanket at a 20% premium over conventional insulation to measure purchase intent.

arguments.name: Smart LED Bulb Purchase Intent Test
arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase decision.
arguments.sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region in the UK and Germany.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the convenience‑focused smart bulb will be at least 15% higher than for a standard LED bulb when convenience benefits are highlighted.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the cost‑saving smart bulb will be at least 15% higher than for a standard LED bulb when energy‑saving benefits are highlighted.

arguments.decision_rule: If the convenience‑focused smart bulb achieves purchase intent ≥ 15% higher than the standard bulb, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing convenience. If the cost‑saving smart bulb achieves purchase intent ≥ 15% higher than the standard bulb, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing cost savings. If neither meets the threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct a limited test (e.g., a choice-based conjoint survey) to validate whether convenience-driven purchase intent exceeds that for a standard LED bulb. If the test meets the 15% threshold, proceed to develop a convenience‑focused smart lighting line; otherwise, maintain the B2B focus.

arguments.decision_rule: If hobbyists' WTP exceeds non-hobbyists' WTP by ≥15% and prestige score is ≥2 points higher, proceed with differentiated hobbyist proposition (T1). If non-hobbyists' WTP exceeds hobbyists' WTP by ≥15% and price importance is ≥2 points higher, keep single range (T2). If both groups are equal, maintain status quo.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Develop a differentiated proposition for hobbyist woodworkers, emphasizing exclusivity, brand prestige, and limited distribution through specialty dealers. arguments.name: Consumer vs Fashion Brand Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a premium, transparent sustainability message about lyocell and modal (e.g., "Lenzing Tencel: 100% organic, traceable, and certified sustainable"). Group B sees a cost‑focused, B2B‑focused message (e.g., "Lenzing provides high‑quality, long‑term fibre contracts for fashion brands"). Both groups view a neutral product description of lyocell and modal.
arguments.sample: 400 participants: 200 self‑identified eco‑conscious shoppers (recruited via sustainability forums) and 200 fashion brands (rec ‑   10 fashion retailers and 5 small‑brand owners) from Europe and North America.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent: binary choice (Would you buy lyocell apparel from Lenzing? Yes/No). Also collect willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) for a sample product (e.g., a T‑shirt).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show at least 15% higher purchase intent than Group B, and WTP will be at least 20% above a baseline of €15 for a T‑shirt.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show at least 15% higher purchase intent than Group A, and WTP will be at least 10% above a baseline of €15 for a T‑shirt.

arguments.decision_rule: If Group A’s purchase intent exceeds Group B’s by ≥ 15 percentage points AND its WTP exceeds Group B’s by ≥ 20%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for eco‑conscious shoppers. arguments.name: Premium vs. Transparent Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with random assignment to one of two messaging conditions.
arguments.sample: 500 adult consumers in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland (n=200 per condition) recruited via an online panel.
arguments.measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary response (yes/no) to a product description of lyocell apparel priced at €50 (condition A) vs. a description emphasizing transparency, ethical sourcing, and brand Tencel (condition B). 2) Willingness to pay: maximum amount (in euros) a respondent would pay for the same apparel under condition A. 3) Sustainability ranking: 1‑10 scale (1‑1  least important, 10‑1  most important) for sustainability when choosing between lyocell and conventional viscose.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A (premium messaging) will generate >=30% purchase intent and higher willingness-to-pay than Condition B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B (transparent messaging) will generate >=30% purchase intent and higher willingness-to-pay than Condition A.

arguments.decision_rule: If purchase intent in Condition A >=30% AND willingness-to-pay in Condition A >=€30, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., premium apparel). If purchase intent in Condition B >=30% AND willingness-to-pay in Condition B >=€30, proceed to develop a proposition focused on transparency and ethical sourcing. If neither meets threshold, no expansion is justified.

arguments.sample: 500 UK adults aged 18-35, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent for the medical messaging (earplug for hearing sensitivity).

arguments.claim: Consumers will adopt Illumina’s consumer proposition because they view genetic testing as a health‑prevention necessity, and they are willing to pay a premium for personalized insights.
arguments.who_benefits: Individual consumers seeking health insights and early‑diagnosis
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of genetic risk factors for diseases and the desire for proactive health management drives purchase decisions.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Illumina captures value through subscription services, data licensing, and premium pricing for comprehensive reports.
assumptions: Consumers trust Illumina’s scientific credibility.
Health‑conscious consumers prioritize genetic data over ancestry or personal‑history.
Price sensitivity is low for health‑focused testing.
predictions: Surveyed health‑conscious consumers will indicate intent to purchase a consumer‑focused test if price is under $200.
Willingness to pay will increase with additional health insights (e.g., cancer risk) beyond ancestry.
Adoption rates will be higher in regions with higher awareness of genetic diseases.

arguments.claim: Consumers will adopt Illumina’s consumer proposition because they view genetic testing as a personal‑development opportunity, seeking to understand their identity, ancestry, and potential future health risks.
arguments.who_benefits: Individuals interested in self‑discovery, ancestry, and proactive health planning
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Growing cultural emphasis on personal narrative and identity, combined with interest in ancestry and health risk assessment, drives purchase decisions.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Illumina captures value through subscription services, data licensing, and premium pricing for comprehensive reports that highlight ancestry and health insights.
assumptions: Consumers value self‑knowledge and storytelling about their background.
Ancestry and identity are important motivators for genetic testing.
Consumers are willing to pay for personalized insights beyond medical outcomes.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase a consumer‑focused test if the report includes ancestry and personal history.
Willingness to pay will be higher for reports that emphasize identity and storytelling.
Adoption rates will be higher in regions with strong cultural emphasis on ancestry.

arguments.quote: Helix will enable individuals to acquire an unprecedented amount of genetic information by providing affordable sequencing and database services for consumer samples brought through third party partners, driving the creation of an ecosystem of consumer applications.

arguments.claim: Consumers will adopt Illumina’s Helix DNA testing because they view it as a health and wellness product, leading them to purchase multiple test kits and associated services.
arguments.who_benefits: Individual consumers seeking health insights and ancestry information.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers perceive testing as a wellness choice rather than a medical necessity, they are more likely to buy multiple kits and pay for additional services like data analysis and reporting.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Illumina captures value through recurring revenue from test kits, subscription services for data analysis, and premium add‑ons such as ancestry reports.
assumptions: Consumers currently view genetic testing primarily as a medical diagnostic tool.
Health‑focused messaging can shift consumer perception.
Affordable pricing for multiple test kits will be accepted.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to purchase multiple Helix kits within 12 months.
Purchase intent will be higher when tested with a health‑focused pitch compared to a medical‑focused pitch.
Repeat purchase rate for additional services (e.g., ancestry reports) will be at least 30%.

arguments.name: Helix Consumer Motivation Test
arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase scenarios.
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self‑reported interest in ancestry.
arguments.measure: 1) Willingness to purchase a single Helix test kit (binary: yes/no). 2) Willingness to purchase multiple test kits (binary: yes/no). 3) Willingness to subscribe to a data‑analysis service (binary: yes/no).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 60% of respondents will indicate willingness to purchase a single test kit when framed as a health‑focused product; willingness to purchase multiple kits will be lower than for ancestry framing.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 60% of respondents will indicate willingness to purchase a single test kit when framed as an ancestry‑focused product; willingness to purchase multiple kits will be higher than for health framing.

arguments.decision_rule: If the health‑focused scenario yields ≥60% willingness to purchase a single kit and the ancestry scenario yields <40% willingness, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition for health. If the ancestry scenario yields ≥60% willingness and the health scenario <40%, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition for ancestry. If neither meets the thresholds, do not expand.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.claim: Consumers will purchase hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory if they perceive it as fashionable and comfortable, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay premium prices.
arguments.who_benefits: Moldex-Metric would benefit by capturing higher margins and expanding its consumer market.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers increasingly view earplugs as fashion items and as a personal care product, not just industrial safety gear.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Premium pricing for stylish designs, direct-to-consumer sales, and brand extension through lifestyle partnerships.
assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with fashion and comfort.
There is a market segment willing to pay for stylish earplugs beyond functional safety needs.
Moldex can design and market a differentiated consumer line without compromising safety standards.
predictions: If a test offers a fashion-oriented earplug line, purchase intent among young adults will be at least 20% higher than a functional safety line.
Willingness to pay for a stylish earplug will be at least 30% above the price of a standard safety model.
Sales conversion rate for the fashion line will be at least 15% higher than for the safety line in a controlled test.

arguments.claim: Consumers will purchase hearing protection as a medical necessity when they are aware of health risks and require compliance with workplace regulations, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay premium prices.
arguments.who_benefits: Moldex-Metric would benefit by selling higher-margin compliance kits and expanding its B2B/medical segment.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Regulatory requirements and health awareness increase demand for hearing protection beyond voluntary use.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Premium pricing for compliance kits, bulk sales to employers, and partnerships with safety training programs.
assumptions: Regulatory bodies require hearing protection for certain workplaces.
Consumers are aware of health risks and need to comply with workplace standards.
Moldex can design and market compliance kits that meet regulatory standards without compromising safety.
predictions: If a test offers a compliance kit line, purchase intent among workers will be at least 25% higher than a functional safety line.
Willingness to pay for a compliance kit will be at least 40% above the price of a standard safety model.
Sales conversion rate for the compliance kit will be at least 20% higher than for the safety line in a controlled test.

arguments.name: Home Monitoring vs. Clinic Visit Preference Survey
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized assignment to either a home-monitoring scenario or a clinic-visit scenario. Participants are recruited via a panel to match demographic and sleep apnoea status (e.g., diagnosed with OSA). They are shown a description of a non-contact sleep sensor (S+ or SleepMinder) and asked to indicate whether they would purchase it and at what price they would consider acceptable. After viewing the description, they are asked about their current method of sleep monitoring (clinic visits vs. home monitoring).
arguments.sample: 400 adults aged 25-65, recruited via an online panel, stratified by sleep apnoea status (diagnosed vs. not diagnosed). Target: 200 per arm.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent: binary (would buy) and maximum price willing to pay. Also, self-reported importance of reducing clinic visits (1‑10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: If the home-monitoring scenario is shown, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than the clinic-visit scenario, and willingness to pay will be lower by $20 compared to the clinic scenario.
prediction_by_theory.T2: If the clinic-visit scenario is shown, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than the home-monitoring scenario, and willingness to pay will be higher by $20 compared to the home scenario.

arguments.decision_rule: If the home-monitoring scenario yields purchase intent ≥ 15% higher than the clinic scenario AND willingness to pay ≤ €150, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition for home use. If the clinic scenario yields higher intent, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

Sales of the drill would be higher in regions with strong gardening culture than in areas where gardening is a minor hobby.

result.excerpt: The children at Westtown knew a good thing when they saw it, to be sure, but not the big buyers like hardware and department stores. To these retailers, the Flexible Flyer looked too different from the familiar sleds and toboggans of their youth.

arguments.claim: Individual gardeners and hobby farmers will adopt a differentiated seed drill for small plots because they need affordable, easy-to-use tools for home gardening and will purchase from a manufacturer that provides direct retail and after‑sale service.
arguments.who_benefits: Home gardeners gain a convenient way to plant seeds without hiring labor; Allen benefits from a new consumer market and recurring revenue.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: In 1888, most gardeners grew their own food on small plots and relied on manual methods. A compact, easy‑to‑use seed drill would eliminate the need for hired labor and reduce the time required to plant, making home gardening more accessible
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Allen would sell the drill directly to consumers through its own retail outlets, capturing a margin on the unit price and generating repeat purchases for parts and service.
assumptions: Home gardeners in 1888 had sufficient disposable income to purchase a seed drill.
Allen could produce a reliable, affordable drill within its manufacturing capacity.
Consumers would trust Allen to provide after‑sale service and support.
predictions: If offered, at least 10% of surveyed home gardeners would express intent to purchase a seed drill within six months.
Sales of the drill would be higher in regions with strong gardening culture than in areas where gardening is a minor hobby.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting outdoor recreation and lifestyle use, using design and comfort as key differentiators. Begin with a willingness-to-pay survey (as proposed in test X1) to validate consumer demand before full product development.
arguments.target_customer: Outdoor enthusiasts, hikers, campers, and users of recreational activities who value comfort and style in hearing protection.
arguments.value_proposition: A hearing protector that combines advanced safety certification with stylish design and ergonomic comfort, positioned as a lifestyle accessory that enhances outdoor experiences while ensuring protection.
arguments.next_action: Run the willingness-to-pay survey (400 participants, 8 weeks, €18,000 budget) to measure demand for a lifestyle proposition.
arguments.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for design and comfort; competitive response from established brands; ability to achieve higher margins without compromising safety standards.
would_change_if: If the survey shows willingness-to-pay below €20 (a €10 premium), indicating insufficient demand to justify investment.
If new evidence shows strong medical demand (e.g., >15% willingness to pay for medical certification) that would shift focus to T2.
If a competitor launches a successful differentiated lifestyle product in the same segment, reducing perceived differentiation value.
